summary: A Lake Michigan pierhead light at the Manistee River mouth: a shore light burned in 1871, the station moved to the north pier in 1894, and a 1927 cast-iron tower now opens for climbs.

lens.where: lantern of the 1927 north pier tower

structures.note: Shore light in a wood-frame house with an attached tower; burned in the autumn of 1871 (cite 3, 2)

Cylindrical cast-iron tower at the end of the north pier; 38 ft per LighthouseFriends (cite 2) and Lakeshore Keepers (cite 9), 39 ft per the USLHS record (cite 1) and the Lighthouse Directory (cite 8); USLHS gives 1925 for the tower (cite 1)

access.note: Reached on foot along the north pier from Fifth Avenue Beach. Closed for the 2026 season; reopens May 21, 2027, per Lakeshore Keepers.

facts.agency: City of Manistee (owner); Lakeshore Keepers (manager, since January 2025); U.S. Coast Guard (operator per the Lighthouse Directory)

events.note: Construction of the first light, a two-story wood-frame house with an attached tower, begins on the north bank
Fifth Order Fresnel lens shown at the opening of the 1870 navigation season (keeper Octavius W. Barney)
Autumn fire destroys the shore light. LighthouseFriends dates it to October 8; Pepper to October 6
Congress appropriates $10,000; the replacement is a duplicate of the original; temporary light shown that fall
Permanent replacement lens installed in the rebuilt shore light
Pierhead beacon lit at the end of the south pier on October 15; the shore light is discontinued and the fifth-order lens moved to the pierhead
Pierhead beacon moved 156 feet to the new end of the extended south pier
Ten-inch steam whistle established on the south pier, February 10, 1890
Pierhead light and fog signal moved from the south pier to the north pier; conduit system built
Conduit removed; fog-signal building moved about 260 feet lakeward (Board) and given a sixth-order lantern; Board entry says the light changed June 1, 1900; LighthouseFriends gives June 9
Municipal electricity; all lights at Manistee electrified
Present cylindrical cast-iron tower erected at the end of the north pier with a fog signal; the fog-signal building and old walkway removed
Fifth-order lens placed in the new tower lantern
Shore light discontinued; its lantern moved to the new tower and the house transferred into private ownership
Lighthouse Bureau and Life-Saving Service combined into the Coast Guard, which took over the Manistee aids
Manistee North Pier listed on the National Register (per the Historic Structures Report)
Elevated walkway declared surplus and transferred to the City of Manistee
Old shore-light house moved to the west end of Second Avenue; now a private residence
Coast Guard declares the North Pierhead Light surplus property
Ownership transferred to the City of Manistee (ceremony June 30, 2011); the HSR gives 2010
State grants $20,000 for a historic structures report on the needed restoration
Exterior repaired and repainted; the Lighthouse Directory says spring, the HSR summer
City Council transfers management to the Sable Points Lighthouse Keepers Association (now Lakeshore Keepers), January 2025
Opened to the public for the first time, per Lakeshore Keepers
Shore (main) light reactivated, June 18, 1894 per LighthouseFriends and Pepper; the HSR narrative says 1893, its chronology says 1894

corrections.proposed: Remove the 1854 tower; the first light here was built 1869-70 on the north bank and burned in 1871
corrections.why: No cited source gives a light here in 1854; the first shore light was built 1869-70 and burned in 1871. The HSR does quote the NRHP listing's period of significance as '1854 to Present' with significant dates 1854, 1875 and 1927, and says an amendment gives ca. 1925 to 1940; neither describes a light built in 1854, so the record's tower entry is unsupported.
No source supports an 1854 building event at this station. The HSR cites 1854 only as the NRHP period-of-significance start, not as a construction date.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends dates the $10,000 allocation to 28 July 1866. Pepper and the HSR say the funds were approved in 1867. The story gives 1867 and notes the disagreement.
LighthouseFriends says 8 October 1871; Pepper says 6 October 1871; the HSR gives only the fall of 1871. The story gives both dates.
LighthouseFriends gives $5,500; Pepper and the HSR give $5,000. The story gives $5,000 and notes the other figure.
USLHS roster 1894-1906; LighthouseFriends and the HSR 1888-1906. Both are printed; the story notes the difference.
USLHS and LighthouseFriends 1941; the HSR table 1939 (end date unsure).
USLHS record: tower established 1925. LighthouseFriends, the HSR and the Lighthouse Directory: 1927. The HSR notes the upper sections of the tower may have come from Chicago's South Breakwater.
HSR: 1914, with the breakwater completed that year. LighthouseFriends: a post lantern in April 1914, replaced by a red skeletal tower in December 1915.
HSR: 2010. LighthouseFriends and the Lighthouse Directory: ceremony and transfer 30 June 2011. The story gives 2011 as the ceremony and notes the HSR date.

The HSR narrative says 1893; its chronology and executive summary say 1894; Pepper and LighthouseFriends give 18 June 1894 (Pepper says the decision was made in 1893). The story gives 1894 and states the HSR's 1893.

The Board report and LighthouseFriends say the fog-signal building moved about 260 feet lakeward; the HSR narrative says the north pier was extended 260 feet and the building moved to its new end. The story gives the Board's version and states the HSR's.
The Board's entry says the light changed on 1 June 1900; the Board's list of changes and LighthouseFriends say 9 June 1900. The story gives both.
LighthouseFriends and Lakeshore Keepers say 38 ft; the USLHS record, the Lighthouse Directory and Pepper say 39 ft. The story gives both.
The HSR gives 1867 for the survey crew that selected the site; Pepper dates a survey of the site to 1876, after construction began in 1869. The story follows the HSR and states Pepper's date.

The Lighthouse Directory says the state granted $20,000 in 2013 for a structures report; the HSR says the museum retained its consultant in 2014 and dates the report 1 September 2016. The sources do not say whether these are one study; the story says so.
The HSR says the upper sections were relocated from Chicago's South Breakwater Tower, but says conclusive evidence remains to be discovered. The story reports both halves.
The Board's 1899 entry says the fog-signal house was damaged by the schooner, then repaired. It does not say collision, so the story uses 'damaged'.

notes_for_editor: Newspapers: Chronicling America searches for Manistee (1870-1880, 1890-1930, 1871) all returned HTTP 520 from loc.gov after retries, so no newspaper pages are cited; the 1871 fire, the 1875 lighting and the 1899 collision rest on the report, LighthouseFriends and Pepper. The 1899 entry says damage, not collision; the story uses 'damaged'. NRHP nomination 90000718 is not digitised (NPGallery says so); the 1990 listing date comes from the HSR. Keeper table in the HSR (printed p. 17, PDF p. 20) was read by column position and checked against the page image on 2026-10-22: Barney, McKee, King (acting), Roberts, Robinson, Hinman, McClure, Hall, Davis dates all match the image. The Light-House Board volume for fiscal 1899 has no page index, so entry 407 is cited by number. Characteristic: the brief's Fl G 6s is not supported by any source read here; the Lighthouse Directory gives a white light, 3 s on and 3 s off, and this is not a Light List characteristic. Keepers appointed after 1960 (Brunet, Willis, Hartman, Post, William F. Davis) appear only as the USLHS roster and HSR print them, in their public role, with no further details. Roster lines were checked against the USLHS page (cite 1), LighthouseFriends' keeper list (cite 2) and the HSR table (cite 3). The sources differ on a few starts: Wissel 1892 (LighthouseFriends, HSR) against 1894 (USLHS); Thomas Robinson 1888 (LighthouseFriends, HSR) against 1894 (USLHS). The roster keeps the HSR and LighthouseFriends dates and notes the USLHS dates. The OCR of the 1894 Board report prints 'tl^e' for 'the'; the story quotes only the words that OCR reads cleanly, and the 459-hour quote reads 'some 459 hours' because the OCR garbles 'in operation'. Pepper's page places the 1927 tower on the south pier and gives 39 ft; the HSR and LighthouseFriends put it on the north pier, and the story follows them. Visitor hours and fees are the Lakeshore Keepers' listing as of 2026-10-22; check before publishing. The Lakeshore Keepers page says the light opened in 2026; the shore house is a private residence and is not open.
